Unlike some earlier sheets, almost the entire sheet is concentrated on one major syllabus block—Paging and page tables—and that block appears prominently in both exam documents. In the more recent Gedächtnisprotokoll, Paging/Memory Management was even described as a comparatively extensive exam problem, involving construction of page tables, logical/physical addresses, unit conversions, and an inverted-page-table question. Paging and address translation

That matches the organization of the summary very closely: the summary’s section “7. Paging und Seitentabellen” starts with pages, frames, address decomposition and page tables, and then covers TLBs, effective access time, direct/inverted tables and multilevel page tables. ibn-zusammenfassung ibn-zusammenfassung ibn-zusammenfassung

Why Aufgabe 2 and Aufgabe 6 stand out
Aufgabe 2 is almost exactly the skill tested in the recent exam protocol. The protocol says that the Paging problem required students to create/fill page tables and determine logical and physical addresses, with PIDs and addresses given. Gedächtnisprotokoll_Klausur_ IB… That is essentially what Aufgabe 2 trains.
The 2016 exam is equally direct. It gives a logical address translated to a physical address, asks for its offset, page index and frame number, and then asks for the corresponding entries of both a normal and an inverted page table. ibn-klausur-2016
So for exam preparation I would treat Aufgabe 2 as mandatory.
Aufgabe 6 is even more striking. The 2016 exam asks for the memory requirement of a normal page table and then for the memory requirement of an inverted page table. ibn-klausur-2016 Moreover, the old 2012 minitest included in the same PDF asks:

maximum memory requirement of a page table without hierarchical tables;
what fraction of physical memory an inverted page table would require. ibn-klausur-2016

That is essentially Übung 5, Aufgabe 6, just with the parameters packaged slightly differently. So this is not merely “the same topic”; it is a historically demonstrated exam question form.


Aufgabe 1: important concept, less important packaging
The point of Aufgabe 1 is to make you understand the structural relationship
\[
\text{page number}\longrightarrow \boxed{\text{page table}}\longrightarrow\text{frame number}.
\]
That is exactly the formulation used in the summary: the page number is the index, and the corresponding page-table entry contains the frame number. ibn-zusammenfassung
The student-residence analogy itself is unlikely to appear verbatim on an exam. But once you strip away the analogy, it tests two important questions:

What does a direct page table actually represent?
Why can a direct page table contain an enormous number of unused entries?

So I would understand it thoroughly but not spend much time rehearsing the dormitory analogy itself.


Aufgabe 3: TLB capacity + locality
This one is more sophisticated. You have a 4 KiB page, 4-byte integers, an array accessed with stride (M), and a TLB containing 64 entries. You have to reason about when successive array accesses hit different pages and when the working set exceeds the TLB capacity. ueb05-ibn-SS2025
The summary explicitly treats the TLB as a cache of page-table entries, including TLB hits/misses and the fact that only a small number of pages tend to be accessed frequently. ibn-zusammenfassung
So the knowledge is definitely syllabus material, but the exact “choose (M) and (N)” formulation looks more like a deeper exercise than a historically observed exam problem. I’d therefore study the reasoning, but not prioritize it above Aufgaben 2 and 6.


Aufgabe 4: TLB and context switches
This question tests an important consequence of the fact that different processes have different page tables.
The summary explicitly says that each process needs its own direct page table because different processes may use the same logical addresses while referring to different data. ibn-zusammenfassung
Therefore stale entries such as
\[
p \rightarrow f_A
\]
from process A cannot normally simply remain valid when process B, which may map the same page (p) to (f_B), starts executing.
The “does this also apply to threads?” part is particularly useful because it checks whether you understand that threads of one process normally share the same address space.
This is a good short conceptual-exam-question style, even though neither of our two exam documents directly asks it.


Aufgabe 5: useful, but supplementary
This is the easiest one to deprioritize. It literally asks you to use the Address Translation Simulator and submit a screenshot. ueb05-ibn-SS2025
The translation process it illustrates is important. The activity itself is not.
For exam preparation I’d classify it:

Supplementary visualization exercise — do once if the mechanism is unclear; otherwise skip during final revision.



Aufgabe 7: very useful calculation pattern
This task combines two things:
\[
\text{expected access time}
\]
and
\[
\text{locality / why TLB hit rates are high}.
\]
The summary explicitly contains an expected-access-time calculation for a TLB:
\[
E[X]=h(1+T)+(1-h)(2+T)
\]
for the simple one-level case, together with the interpretation of TLB hit and miss costs. ibn-zusammenfassung
Aufgabe 7 generalizes essentially the same reasoning to a (k)-level page table. ueb05-ibn-SS2025
That makes it quite valuable: it is not merely memorizing a formula—you need to reconstruct the formula from the number of memory accesses.
I would therefore consider it strong exam preparation, even though our two exam samples do not show this exact question.


Aufgabe 8: multilevel tables
This is the sheet’s most comprehensive page-table-structure problem. You have to divide a 32-bit logical address among:

page offset,
level-1 index,
level-2 index,
level-3 index,

and then determine the number of table entries and total maximum memory usage. ueb05-ibn-SS2025
The summary explicitly expects understanding of this structure: upper levels contain addresses of lower-level page tables, while only the lowest level plays the role of the ordinary direct page table. ibn-zusammenfassung
So this is core syllabus material. Its only downside from an exam-preparation perspective is that the exercise is rather extensive. An actual exam might split it into smaller subquestions.



My exam-preparation grouping
If we use the same practical categories we were using for the previous sheets, I would group them approximately like this:

And one especially useful conclusion from this sheet is that “Paging und Seitentabellen” should be treated as a major exam block rather than a peripheral chapter. The 2016 exam allocated 12/52 points to Speicherverwaltung, with almost the entire problem centered on page tables. ibn-klausur-2016 The newer memory protocol again reports a large Paging/Memory-Management problem involving page tables, address translation, size calculations, and inverted page tables. 3. Counting processes
Every process that reaches a successful fork() creates one additional process.
Thus, if there are (k) processes immediately before a fork() and all (k) execute it successfully, there will be
\[
2k
\]
processes afterwards.
For \(n\) successive unconditional calls,
fork();
fork();
fork();
the total number is
\[
2^n.
\]
Here, three calls produce \(2^3=8\) processes, including the original process.
This shortcut works only when every existing process executes every call. With conditions, loops, exit(), or exec(), you must trace the individual execution paths.

title: 3  Processes and fork()
text:
4. The safe process-tree method
For each fork():

Identify every process that reaches the call.
Give each of them one new child.
Copy the parent’s current variable values into the child.
Assign the appropriate return value:

parent receives a positive PID;
child receives zero.

Continue tracing every resulting process separately.

Do not count the number of occurrences of the word fork and immediately use \(2^n\). A conditional call may be reached by only part of the process tree.

Example
pid_t p = fork();

if (p == 0)
    fork();
After the first call:

parent: p > 0;
child: p == 0.

Only the child enters the if and executes the second call. Consequently, there are three processes, not four.

title: 3  Processes and fork()
text:
5. Process hierarchy
Each child has:

its own PID;
the PID of its parent, called its PPID.

This produces a process tree. A child created later by an existing child becomes a grandchild of the original process.
The parent and child normally execute concurrently. The scheduler may run either one first, so the order of their output is generally not predictable.
However, the order of instructions inside one process remains fixed.

title: 3  Processes and fork()
text:
6. The five basic process states
The five-state model required by the course is: 01-ibn-zusammenfassung.pdf







State
Meaning




New
The process is being created.


Ready
It can execute but is waiting for a CPU.


Running
Its instructions are currently being executed by a CPU.


Waiting / Blocked
It cannot continue until some event occurs, such as completion of I/O.


Terminated
It has finished execution or has been terminated.



The important distinction is:

Ready: capable of running, but no CPU currently assigned;
Waiting: not capable of continuing yet, even if a CPU were available.


State transitions



Transition
Typical cause




New → Ready
The process is admitted into the ready queue


Ready → Running
The scheduler dispatches it


Running → Ready
Time slice expires or the process is preempted


Running → Waiting
It requests I/O or waits for an event


Waiting → Ready
I/O completes or the awaited event occurs


Running → Terminated
It finishes or calls exit()



Normally, a process does not move directly from Waiting to Running. Once its event occurs, it becomes Ready and waits to be selected by the scheduler.


Where does fork() fit?
A parent must be Running to execute fork(). The operating system creates a child, which passes through New and becomes Ready. The scheduler then decides whether the parent or the child runs next.
Calling fork() does not guarantee that the child executes first.

title: 3  Processes and fork()

7. Common exam traps

Counting only the children and forgetting the original parent.
Assuming that only the child continues after fork().
Reversing the return values: the child gets 0; the parent gets the child’s PID.
Assuming the parent always runs before the child.
Forgetting that descendants inherit the current value of previously assigned variables.
Using (2^n) even though some calls are conditional.
Confusing Ready with Waiting.
Claiming that I/O completion causes Waiting → Running directly.

title: 4  Race conditions, semaphores and synchronization
text:
Race conditions
A race condition exists when the correctness or result of a program unintentionally depends on the timing or execution order of concurrent operations.
A typical race condition requires:

shared state;
concurrent accesses to that state;
at least one access that modifies it;
insufficient synchronization.

The output may differ between executions because the scheduler can produce different interleavings.

Critical region
A critical region or critical section is a part of a program that accesses shared data and must not be executed simultaneously with a conflicting critical region.
entry protocol

critical region

exit protocol

non-critical region
The entry and exit protocols are implemented using a mutex, semaphore or another synchronization primitive.


Requirements of a good mutual-exclusion solution
A correct solution should provide:

Mutual exclusion: conflicting threads are never simultaneously inside their critical regions.
Progress: a thread outside its critical region must not unnecessarily prevent others from entering.
No timing assumptions: correctness must not depend on CPU speed or the number of cores.
No starvation/bounded waiting: a thread requesting entry should not be postponed forever.

The first is a safety property: “nothing bad happens.” Progress and absence of starvation are liveness properties: “something good eventually happens.”

Atomicity
An operation is atomic if other threads cannot observe or interrupt a partially completed execution of that operation.
For example, the abstract operation
wait(S)
must itself be atomic. If two threads could simultaneously test and decrement the semaphore non-atomically, the semaphore would not provide synchronization.
Protecting a critical region does not mean that all its ordinary instructions become individually atomic. It means that the entry protocol ensures that only the permitted thread or threads can execute that region.

title: 4  Race conditions, semaphores and synchronization
text:
Semaphores
A semaphore contains:

a nonnegative count representing available permits or resource instances;
an associated queue of blocked threads;
two atomic operations, conventionally called wait and signal.

Other common names are:



Operation
Alternative names




wait(S)
P(S), down(S), sem_wait(S)


signal(S)
V(S), up(S), post(S), sem_post(S)




wait(S)
Conceptually:
if a permit is available:
    consume one permit
    continue
else:
    block until a permit becomes available
Thus, wait may block.


signal(S)
Conceptually:
make one permit available
if a thread is waiting:
    wake one waiting thread
signal does not normally block.
The implementation may represent blocked threads using negative values or separate queues, but exam solutions should normally describe the abstract behaviour rather than depend on a particular representation.


Binary and counting semaphores
A binary semaphore has at most one available permit:
Semaphore mutex = 1
A counting semaphore can represent several identical resource instances:
Semaphore printers = 3
Up to three successful wait(printers) operations can occur before another thread must release a permit.

title: 4  Race conditions, semaphores and synchronization
text:
Mutual exclusion with a semaphore
Initialize the semaphore to 1:
Semaphore mutex = 1
Every thread uses:
wait(mutex)

    // critical region

signal(mutex)
The first thread consumes the only permit. Other threads calling wait(mutex) must block until the first thread calls signal(mutex).
The protected operation must lie entirely between wait and signal:
wait(mutex)
counter = counter + 1
signal(mutex)
Protecting only the load or only the store would still allow an unsafe interleaving.

Mutex versus binary semaphore
At the level required by many introductory exercises, a mutex can be viewed as a binary lock. More precisely:

a mutex normally has an owner;
only the thread that locked it should unlock it;
a semaphore represents permits and does not necessarily have ownership.

Semaphores can consequently express both mutual exclusion and dependencies between different threads.

title: 4  Race conditions, semaphores and synchronization
text:
Enforcing an execution order
Suppose block X in Thread 1 may execute only after block Y in Thread 2.
Initialize a semaphore to zero:
Semaphore finished_Y = 0
Thread 1:
wait(finished_Y)
X
Thread 2:
Y
signal(finished_Y)
Why initialize it to zero?

If Thread 1 reaches wait first, it blocks.
After Thread 2 completes Y, signal provides the permit.
If Thread 2 finishes first, the semaphore retains the permit. Thread 1’s later wait consumes it and continues immediately.

This is what is meant by saying that a semaphore has memory: an earlier signal can be remembered in its counter.

title: 4  Race conditions, semaphores and synchronization
text:
Blocking versus busy waiting
A primitive can wait in two ways.

Busy waiting
while lock is unavailable:
    repeatedly test lock
The thread remains runnable and consumes CPU time. A lock implemented this way is often called a spinlock.
Busy waiting can be reasonable for extremely short waits inside kernels or multiprocessor code, but it is inefficient for long waits.


Blocking
If the resource is unavailable:

the thread is placed in a waiting queue;
its state becomes Waiting/Blocked;
another runnable thread receives the CPU;
a later signal makes the blocked thread Ready.

Notice that waking a thread normally produces:
Waiting → Ready
not immediately Waiting → Running.

title: 4  Race conditions, semaphores and synchronization
text:
Condition variables
A condition variable allows a thread to sleep until some condition involving shared state may have become true.
It must be used together with:

a predicate, such as count > 0 or production_done;
a mutex protecting that predicate;
the condition variable on which threads wait.

Canonical pattern:
lock(mutex)

while (!condition) {
    cond_wait(condition_variable, mutex)
}

// condition is true; access shared state

unlock(mutex)
cond_wait(cv, mutex) performs three important actions:

atomically releases mutex and puts the caller to sleep;
waits for a notification;
reacquires mutex before returning.

The atomic release-and-sleep step prevents the following lost-wakeup race:

waiter checks that the condition is false;
notifier makes it true and sends a signal;
waiter goes to sleep after the signal;
no future signal arrives.


Why while, not if?
After waking, the thread must check the predicate again because:

wakeups may be spurious;
another awakened thread may acquire the mutex first and consume the resource;
a notification means “the condition may now be true,” not “the condition is guaranteed to remain true.”

Correct:
while (count == 0)
    cond_wait(not_empty, mutex)
Unsafe:
if (count == 0)
    cond_wait(not_empty, mutex)


signal versus broadcast

cond_signal(cv) wakes at least one waiting thread.
cond_broadcast(cv) wakes all threads waiting on cv.

A producer adding one item normally needs to wake only one consumer. If production_done becomes true and every consumer must notice it and terminate, a broadcast is appropriate.
The awakened threads do not all enter the critical region simultaneously: each must first reacquire the mutex.


Condition variables do not remember notifications
If cond_signal or cond_broadcast is called while nobody is waiting, the notification disappears.
This differs from a semaphore:
signal(S)
with no waiter increments or preserves the semaphore’s permit count, so a later wait(S) can consume it.
A mutex remembers whether it is currently locked, but an unlock is not a stored notification that a future thread can consume.


Why update and signal under the mutex?
The standard protocol is:
lock(mutex)
done = true
cond_broadcast(done_changed)
unlock(mutex)
The mutex makes changing the predicate and notifying waiters part of one synchronized protocol. A waiter cannot slip between checking done and beginning to wait. When it wakes and reacquires the mutex, it sees a consistent value of done.


Example: producer-consumer queue

producers create items / jobs and insert them into a shared queue.
consumers remove items
a consumer cannot remove an item while the queue is empty
instead of repeatedly checking the queue in a busy loop, it sleeps on not_empty


Concrete Example: downloading and playing a video
The producer downloads video chunks:
network -> buffer
The consume decodes and siplays them
buffer -> video player

the downloader puts some chunks into the buffer
the player begins consuming them
both continue concurrently

Other canonical examples:

a network interface receives packets, while an application processes them
a web server accepts requests while worker threads handle earlier requests
one thread reads files, while another processes their contents.
keyboard input arriving while the application processe earlier input

The general pattern is that

a buffer crates a pipleline and absorbs temporary differences in speed between producers and consumers



Benefits of concurrent production and consumption

lower latency: the consumer can start as soon as the first item exists instead of waiting for all items
higher throughput: production and consumption may overlap

one core produces while another consumes
a network or disk operation runs while the cpu processes previous data

bounded memory use: for a large or infinite stream, we may use a bounded buffer:
producer -> fixed-size buffer -> consumer
A bounded buffer typically uses two predicates and two condition variables:
std::condition_variable not_empty; // consumers wait here
std::condition_variable not_full; // producers wait here




Complete producer-consumer program
shared Queue jobs
shared Mutex mutex
shared ConditionVariable not_empty
shared Boolean production_done = false

function producer():
    for number from 1 to 10:
        job = create_job(number)

        lock(mutex) //begin critical region 1

        jobs.push(job)
        signal(not_empty)

        unlock(mutex)

        // end critical region 1

    // no more jobs will be produced
    lock(mutex) // begin critical region 2

    production_done = true
    broadcast(not_empty)

    unlock(mutex) // end cr 2

function consumer(worker_id):
    while true:
        lock(mutex)

        while jobs.empty() and not production_done:
            wait(not_empty, mutex)
        
        if jobs.empty() and production_done:
            unlock(mutex)
            return
        
        job = jobs.pop()

        unlock(mutex)

        // processing is done outside of critical region
        process(job)

function main():
    producer_thread = start_thread(producer)
    consumer_thread_1 = start_thread(consumer, 1)
    consumer_thread_2 = start_thread(consumer, 2)

    join(producer_thread)
    join(consumer_thread_1)
    join(consumer_thread_2)

    print("all jobs completed")


Bounded-buffer producer-consumer problem
uses a shared queue with a fixed maximum capacity

consumers wait on not_empty when the buffer is empty
producers wait on not_full when the buffer is full
a mutex protexts the buffer and related shared state

The bounded buffer provides backpressure: if consumers cannot keep up, producers are forced to wait instead of allowing the queue to grow indefiniely.

Practical Example
Consider a program that reads large imagems from disk and processes them:

the producer reads images and places them in memory
several consumers resize / transform or analyze the images
each image may occupy considerable memory

An unbounded queue could consumer all abailable memory if disk reading is temporarily faster than image processing. A buffer limited to, say, five images ensures that at most five unprocessed images are held in memory


Complete typed pseudocode

// shared state

constant BUFFER_CAPACITY = 5
constant NUMBER_OF_JOBS = 20
constant NUMBER_OF_CONSUMERS = 2

shared Queue<Job> jobs

shared Mutex mutex
shared ConditionVarialbe not_empty
shared ConditionVarialbe not_full

shared production_done = false


// producer
function producer() -> Void:
    for job_number from 1 to NUMBER_OF_JOBS:
        job = new Job(job_number)

        lock(mutex)

        while jobs.size() == BUFFER_CAPACITY:
            wait(not_full, mutex)
        
        // buffer is not full
        jobs.push(job)

        // buffer is not empty
        signal(not_empty)
        
        unlock(mutex)

    lock(mutex)

    production_done = true
    // every sleeping consumer must discover that production is finished
    broadcast(not_empty)

    unlock(mutex)

// consumer

function consumer() -> Void:
    while true:
        lock(mutex)

        while jobs.empty() and not production_done:
            wait(not_empty, mutex)
        
        // no buffered jobs remain, and no new jobs will arrive
        if jobs.empty() and production_done:
            unlock(mutex)
            return

        // buffer not empty
        job = jobs.pop()

        // at least one producer may now be able to proceed
        signal(not_full)

        unlock(mutex)

        process(job)


// main program

function main() -> Void:
    consumers = new Array<Thread>(NUMBER_OF_CONSUMERS)

    for i from 0 to NUMBER_OF_CONSUMERS - 1:
        consumers[i] = start_thread(consumer)

    producer_thread = start_thread(producer)

    join(producer_thread)
    
    for i in [1, NUMBER_OF_CONSUMERS]:
        join(consumers[i])

    print("all jobs completed")






join()



join() does not end the thread. It makes the calling thread wait until another thread has finished.
consumer_thread_1 = start_thread(consume, 1)

... 

join(consumer_thread_1)

start a new htread executing consumer(1)
continue executing the main thread
When join(consumer_thread_1) is reached, pause the main thread until consumer_thread_1 terminates

This guarantees that the main thread will not prematurely terminate before consumer_thread_1 does, which would be possible because the scheduler can decide to execute the return or the final statement of main, ending the main thread, before consumer_thread_1 is finished

text:
Producer–consumer pattern
For a bounded buffer of capacity (N), a semaphore solution uses:
Semaphore empty = N
Semaphore full  = 0
Semaphore mutex = 1
Producer:
produce(item)

wait(empty)
wait(mutex)
insert(item)
signal(mutex)
signal(full)
Consumer:
wait(full)
wait(mutex)
item = remove()
signal(mutex)
signal(empty)

consume(item)
Interpretation:

empty counts free slots;
full counts stored items;
mutex protects the buffer data structure.

Do not acquire mutex before waiting for empty or full. Otherwise a thread might sleep while holding the buffer lock, preventing the other side from changing the condition it is waiting for.

title: 4  Race conditions, semaphores and synchronization
text:
Simplified read–write lock
Suppose:
Semaphore S = N
A reader consumes one permit:
lock_read:
    wait(S)

unlock_read:
    signal(S)
A writer attempts to consume all (N) permits:
lock_write:
    repeat N times:
        wait(S)

unlock_write:
    repeat N times:
        signal(S)
This appears to permit either:

up to (N) simultaneous readers; or
one writer holding every permit.

But lock_write is not atomic.
For (N=3), two writers could execute:
W1: wait(S)   // S: 3 → 2
W2: wait(S)   // S: 2 → 1
W1: wait(S)   // S: 1 → 0
W2: wait(S)   // blocks
W1: wait(S)   // blocks
Neither writer can acquire all three permits, and neither can release its partial acquisition because it has not entered the critical region. This is a deadlock.
A simple repair serializes writers while they collect the permits:
Semaphore S = N
Semaphore writer_gate = 1

lock_write:
    wait(writer_gate)
    repeat N times:
        wait(S)
    signal(writer_gate)

unlock_write:
    repeat N times:
        signal(S)
Only one writer may now attempt the multi-step acquisition.
This repair prevents the writer–writer split deadlock, but it does not necessarily guarantee fairness: continuously arriving readers might still starve a writer.
One correction to retain from your earlier work: your old Sheet 3 answer identified the interleaved writer acquisition, but described it as permitting simultaneous writing. The direct consequence is instead the deadlock shown above. 14-Operating-Systems-and-Networs-SoSe-25-Solutions.pdf

text:
Common exam traps

Treating counter++ as an indivisible operation.
Thinking a race requires multiple CPU cores.
Protecting different threads with different mutexes.
Forgetting to initialize a mutex semaphore to 1.
Initializing an ordering semaphore to 1 instead of 0.
Forgetting that semaphore operations must themselves be atomic.
Omitting signal on some control-flow path.
Sleeping while holding a mutex needed by the thread that could wake you.
Using if instead of while around cond_wait.
Assuming condition-variable notifications are remembered.
Confusing deadlock with starvation.
Calling every timing-dependent output a race: nondeterministic ordering can be intentional and harmless.

Exam-like exercises
Do these closed-book. Allow approximately 35–45 minutes in total.

Exercise 1: Race condition and semaphore repair
Two threads share:
integer counter = 0
Thread A:
repeat 3 times:
    counter = counter + 1
Thread B:
repeat 2 times:
    counter = counter + 1
Assume a single-core system and that an increment consists of:
LOAD counter into private register R
ADD 1 to R
STORE R into counter

Questions

Define the term race condition.
What should the final value of counter be?
Give an instruction-level interleaving in which one update is lost.
Explain why the race can occur despite there being only one CPU core.
Repair the program using one semaphore. State its initial value.
Explain completely but concisely what wait and signal do.
Would it be sufficient for A and B to use two different mutexes? Explain.

Exercise 2: Ordering and condition variables

Part A: Ordering
Block send_result in Thread A may execute only after Thread B has completed calculate_result.
Write the simplest semaphore-based pseudocode for both threads. Give the semaphore’s initial value.
Your solution must work regardless of which thread starts first.


Part B: Find the condition-variable errors
A consumer uses:
lock(mutex)

if (count == 0)
    cond_wait(not_empty, mutex)

item = remove_from_buffer()
count = count - 1

unlock(mutex)
The producer uses:
add_to_buffer(item)
count = count + 1
cond_signal(not_empty)
Answer:

Identify at least two synchronization errors.
Rewrite the relevant consumer and producer pseudocode correctly.
Why must the consumer test the condition in a while loop?
What happens if cond_signal(not_empty) is called while nobody is waiting?
What would happen in the analogous situation with signal(S) on a semaphore?
When would broadcast be preferable to signal?




Exercise 3: Debugging a semaphore construction
Let (N=4):
Semaphore S = 4

lock_read:
    wait(S)

unlock_read:
    signal(S)

lock_write:
    for i = 1 to 4:
        wait(S)

unlock_write:
    for i = 1 to 4:
        signal(S)

Give an exact execution involving two writers that leads to failure.
Classify the failure as:

mutual-exclusion violation,
deadlock, or
starvation.

Explain precisely why neither writer can continue.
Repair the construction using one additional semaphore or mutex.
Does your repair also guarantee that a writer can never starve? Explain briefly.
